**Instructions.** Choose the single best answer (a–e) for each question. You may use a periodic table.
Calculators are allowed. Answers are rounded to the precision shown. Time yourself: aim for about 30 minutes
(roughly 2 minutes per question, the same pace as the full exam). **Solubility rules are not provided:** work from memory, as on the exam.

**Answer sheet.** Use the bubble answer sheet (`CHEM1301/exam-prep/answer-sheet/answer-sheet.pdf`), rows 1–15.

```{=latex}
\needspace{9\baselineskip}
```
**1.** Table 7.1 calls some salts "slightly soluble." According to the course, how does that compare with "insoluble"?

```{=latex}
\begingroup\leftskip=1.5em
```
a)\ Insoluble salts are strong electrolytes; slightly soluble salts are not\
b)\ Slightly soluble means more than half of the salt dissolves\
c)\ Slightly soluble salts never form precipitates\
d)\ They mean the same thing: so little dissolves that it can't be detected with the naked eye\
e)\ Slightly soluble salts dissolve completely if the solution is stirred

```{=latex}
\par\endgroup\medskip
```

```{=latex}
\needspace{9\baselineskip}
```

**4.** Which solubility rule explains why Na~2~S is **soluble** in water?

```{=latex}
\begingroup\leftskip=1.5em
```
a)\ Rule 3: most chlorides are soluble, except AgCl, PbCl~2~, and Hg~2~Cl~2~\
b)\ Rule 1: most nitrate (NO~3~^−^) salts are soluble\
c)\ Rule 6: most sulfides, carbonates, and phosphates are only slightly soluble\
d)\ Rule 5: most hydroxides are only slightly soluble (NaOH and KOH are the exceptions)\
e)\ Rule 2: most salts of Na^+^, K^+^, and NH~4~^+^ are soluble

```{=latex}
\par\endgroup\medskip
```

```{=latex}
\needspace{9\baselineskip}
```

c)\ Rule 6: most sulfides, carbonates, and phosphates are only slightly soluble\
d)\ Rule 2: most salts of Na^+^, K^+^, and NH~4~^+^ are soluble\

**9.** Which is the balanced **molecular** equation for mixing aqueous BaCl~2~ and K~2~SO~4~?

```{=latex}
\begingroup\leftskip=1.5em
```
a)\ BaCl~2~(aq) + K~2~SO~4~(aq) $\rightarrow$ BaSO~4~(s) + 2KCl(aq)\
b)\ BaCl~2~(aq) + K~2~SO~4~(aq) $\rightarrow$ BaSO~4~(aq) + 2KCl(aq)\
c)\ No reaction (NR)\
d)\ BaCl~2~(aq) + K~2~SO~4~(aq) $\rightarrow$ BaSO~4~(aq) + 2KCl(s)\
e)\ BaCl~2~(aq) + K~2~SO~4~(aq) $\rightarrow$ BaSO~4~(s) + KCl(aq)

```{=latex}
\par\endgroup\medskip
```

```{=latex}
\needspace{9\baselineskip}
```

**12.** Aqueous solutions of iron(III) nitrate and sodium hydroxide are mixed. What is the **net ionic** equation?

```{=latex}
\begingroup\leftskip=1.5em
```
a)\ Fe^3+^(aq) + 3OH^−^(aq) $\rightarrow$ Fe(OH)~3~(s)\
b)\ Na^+^(aq) + NO~3~^−^(aq) $\rightarrow$ NaNO~3~(s)\
c)\ No reaction occurs (NR)\
d)\ Fe^3+^(aq) + OH^−^(aq) $\rightarrow$ Fe(OH)~3~(s)\
e)\ Fe^3+^(aq) + 3NO~3~^−^(aq) + 3Na^+^(aq) + 3OH^−^(aq) $\rightarrow$ Fe(OH)~3~(s) + 3Na^+^(aq) + 3NO~3~^−^(aq)

```{=latex}
\par\endgroup\medskip
```

```{=latex}
\needspace{9\baselineskip}
```

**15.** When K~2~CrO~4~(aq) and Ba(NO~3~)~2~(aq) are mixed, a yellow solid forms. Why can't that solid be made of only K^+^ and Ba^2+^ ions?

```{=latex}
\begingroup\leftskip=1.5em
```
a)\ Only nitrate ions can form solids with Ba^2+^\
b)\ Potassium salts are always soluble, so K^+^ can't be in a solid\
c)\ Ba^2+^ never forms solids, so the solid must contain K^+^\
d)\ A solid compound must have zero net charge, so it needs both a cation and an anion\
e)\ K^+^ and Ba^2+^ have different charges, so they can't fit in one crystal

```{=latex}
\par\endgroup\medskip
```
